title: Monitorable-by-design architectures for a post-Astra world: a compartmentalization-based approach
authors: Jake Watts, Joel Sokol
abstract: Frontier models like GPT-6 Astra are increasingly able to do substantial reasoning without a monitorable chain of thought, chains of thought are becoming less legible, and are often monitored asynchronously to reduce cost. With the future of chain of thought monitoring unclear, it may be necessary to design LLMs with monitorability in mind. We propose a modification to existing LLM architectures based on GRAM, SGTM, DEMix, BTS, and similar methods to compartmentalize dangerous capabilities so th

title: LUCID: Statistically Grounded Self-Correction for LLM Reasoning Evaluation
authors: Satiyabooshan Murugaboopathy, Adel Daoud, Connor T. Jerzak
abstract: Cheap language-model raters grade chain-of-thought reasoning at scale, yet systematic step-rating errors can skew reasoning audits and solution rankings. We introduce LUCID (Loop for Unbiased Calibration via Inference-time Diagnosis), which pairs prompt self-correction with Design-based Supervised Learning (DSL). title: SwiftLoop: Selective Refinement for Adaptive Implicit Reasoning in Looped Transformers
authors: Tianyi Zhao, Ke Wan, Chen Chen
abstract: Looped Transformers advance implicit chain-of-thought reasoning through recurrent latent refinement. However, existing looped reasoners typically employ fixed-depth recurrence, updating all latent positions at every iteration and incurring redundancy when further refinement is unnecessary. title: Look Before You Commit: Visual-Evidence-Guided Decoding for Multimodal Diffusion Language Models
authors: Tongxiao Hu, Yikai Zhao, Qiyan Zhao et al.
abstract: Diffusion multimodal large language models rely on confidence to decide when to commit candidate tokens during generation. In multimodal tasks, however, confidence cannot distinguish whether a candidate originates from image evidence or the language prior. title: Beyond Static Charts: Benchmarking Interactive Chart-to-Code Generation for MLLMs
authors: Yuhan Bian, Haoyu Liu, Siyu Li et al.
abstract: In recent years, multimodal large language models (MLLMs) have achieved significant progress in chart-to-code generation. However, existing benchmarks mainly focus on static charts, overlooking interactive charts that enable richer and more expressive data exploration. Unlike static chart-to-code generation, which emphasizes visual consistency, interactive chart-to-code evaluation targets behavioral consistency, requiring chart states to evolve correctly under sequences of user interactions, the

title: Frequency-Conditioned Privacy Auditing of Fine-Tuned Language Models
authors: Aymen Noor, Ke Lyu, Honglu Jiang
abstract: Large language models are increasingly fine-tuned on sensitive data, where the same person's information may appear multiple times across records. This can cause models to memorize sensitive information, but memorization does not necessarily mean that the information can be recovered. A more serious privacy risk arises when the model begins to reproduce that information during generation. title: Tempering and few-shot calibration of pathology foundation models improve digital biomarker reproducibility across slide scanners
authors: Frank T Wen, Kyler Rosen, Siddhi Ramesh et al.
abstract: Pathology foundation models underpin a growing number of histology-based cancer biomarkers, but sensitivity to slide scanner-specific image signatures degrades cross-center reliability and reproducibility. We developed a foundation model fine-tuning method that improved consistency in head-and-neck cancer human papillomavirus (HPV) prediction, colorectal cancer microsatellite instability (MSI) identification, prostate cancer grading and breast cancer phenotyping. This tempering method decreased

title: Can LLM-Simulated Respondents Pre-Test Survey Questions? Evidence From Preregistered Prospective Validation
authors: Sristi Bafna, Mac MacComas, Michael Bader et al.
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) can be conditioned to simulate behavioral responses, including survey responses, but it remains unclear whether and how these simulations can support downstream research tasks. Here, we evaluate whether simulated respondents can support pre-testing new candidate survey questions before fielding them, operationalized as prioritizing candidate survey items. Specifically, we rank candidate questions by their mean responses, which can reveal ceiling or floor effects; the

title: Reading Between the Layers: Where Representation Quality Lives, and What Geometry Reveals
authors: Arnesh Batra, Aniket Khandelwal, Arush Gumber et al.
abstract: Representation quality in pretrained text foundation models is not concentrated at the final layer, yet practitioners routinely probe it there because layer selection without labels has remained an open problem. We present a large-scale empirical study of where layer quality lives across 25 models spanning four architectural families and four pretraining strategies, evaluated on 13 datasets across classification, pair classification, semantic textual similarity, and multiple-choice question answ

title: A dataset of clinically similar image pairs from citation-linked case reports for medical image retrieval
authors: Guy Shmueli, Keno K. Bressem, Tom Hope
abstract: Retrieving images of patients clinically similar to a given patient can support diagnosis, teaching and research. Training and evaluating retrieval systems requires knowing which images of different patients show the same finding, and existing datasets are small or narrow in scope. We construct PMC-PaIR, a dataset of 86,144 pairs of clinically similar images from 56,013 open-access PubMed Central case reports, which often document rare or challenging presentations. title: Leaks by Installments: Cross-Session Answer Disclosure in LLM Tutors and a Ledger-Based Defense
authors: Venkata Muttineni, Karthik Narayan, Christopher David
abstract: Tutors built on large language models (LLMs) are told not to give away answers, but a learner does not have to ask for the answer all at once. Existing safeguards judge each reply within the current conversation, so a learner can open a new session, reword the problem, or request a worked solution to the same problem with different numbers. title: Layer-Readout Interfaces in EEG Foundation Models: Predictive Accessibility and Cross-Dataset Transfer
authors: Yanlin Fu, Wei Liu, Liming Zhao
abstract: Intermediate layers often outperform final layers when foundation models are used as frozen feature extractors, but the source of this advantage is unclear. We study this question in EEG foundation models by separating three factors: how representations are read out, whether intermediate layers provide predictive utility beyond the final-layer interface, and whether useful depth structure transfers across datasets. Across five models and three tasks, improving the final-layer readout consistentl

title: Nemotron-Labs-VisualCreation: Pixel as Code for Agentic Visual Creation
authors: Guo Chen, Fuxiao Liu, Haoqin Tu et al.
abstract: Visual creation demands expressive imagery together with precise control over text, layout, and structure. We introduce Nemotron-Labs-VisualCreation, an agentic framework that connects these capabilities through Pixel as Code. Raster images are represented by learned discrete visual tokens, while structured artifacts use explicit programs. title: COGENT: A Modular Cognitive Architecture for Agentic User Simulation
authors: Yikun Chi, Adam Davies, Debarati Das et al.
abstract: LLM-based user simulation can support interface design, accessibility research, and interactive-agent evaluation, but standard computer-use agents are optimized for task completion rather than reproducing how people perceive, reason, and act. We introduce COGENT (COGnitive agENT), a modular cognitive architecture for simulating user interaction with desktop interfaces. title: Who Makes the Decision? Auditing an Agentic LLM Pipeline for Illicit Cryptocurrency Transaction Monitoring
authors: Vaishnavi Chaughule, Yuchen Zhang, Mohammed Ahnaf Tajwar et al.
abstract: Agentic pipelines that combine graph detectors, deterministic rules, retrieval-augmented generation and an LLM judge are being proposed to monitor illicit cryptocurrency flows and to write regulation-citing justifications for analysts. They are evaluated on end-to-end accuracy or on the quality of those justifications, and neither shows which component made a decision. title: LLM-Based Assistant for Dog Care Guidance
authors: Abubakar Sadiq Shittu, Venkat Gopu, Arshita Sharma et al.
abstract: This study investigates whether domain grounding through Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) and parameter-efficient fine-tuning using Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) can enhance the accuracy and reliability of pet care advice generated by large language models (LLMs). We curated a dataset of breed-specific dog care information and used it to develop two systems: a RAG pipeline based on TinyLlama-1.1B-Chat-v1.0, and a fine-tuned LLaMA-3.2-1B model adapted using LoRA. title: Can Vibe Coding Produce Accessible Websites: An Empirical Study on LLM Coding Agents and Skills
authors: Syed Fatiul Huq, Md. Asif Haider, Abu Jafar Saifullah et al.
abstract: Large language model (LLM) coding agents increasingly allow developers and non-professionals to create websites through natural-language instructions, with limited inspection of the generated source code. Although this ``vibe coding'' workflow lowers barriers to software creation, it may also propagate accessibility defects at scale. We investigate the accessibility of websites generated end-to-end by contemporary coding agents and whether agent-level accessibility interventions improve their ou

title: Admitted Is Not Effective: Lessons from a Notary-Gated Retrospective Loop in an Agentic Pipeline
authors: Lo Gullstrand Heander, Emma Söderberg, Christofer Rydenfält
abstract: Agentic software development pipelines with frozen prompts can repeat the same mistakes across pull requests (PRs), yet ungoverned additions to instruction files grow without bound and do not generally improve task success. We present a retrospective loop for a four-stage large language model (LLM) pipeline in which a Retrospective agent proposes edits to learned rules every ten PRs and a Notary admits, merges, or rejects them while recording each decision in a provenance ledger. In a pre-regist

title: Fin-RSI: A Unified Library of Financial Skills, Checks, and Self-Improvement for LLM Agents
authors: Wanghao Ye, Shwai He, Sihan Chen et al.
abstract: As large language models (LLMs) become more capable, financial agents need tools they can readily discover and use. Yet financial software is fragmented across libraries with different interfaces and conventions, making it difficult to build reliable agent workflows. We present Fin-RSI, a unified Python library of financial skills, checks, and self-improvement designed for LLM agents. title: Wactorz: Self-Writing LLM Agents That Discover, Repair, and Migrate at the Edge
authors: Panagiotis Kasnesis, Lazaros Toumanidis, Amalia Contiero Syropoulou et al.
abstract: Most LLM agent frameworks build a crew that runs a task and exits. Physical environments (e.g., homes, labs, factory floors) need agents that stay up for months, survive their own bugs, and run on whatever hardware is already next to the sensors. title: Weight Coding: Evolving Web-Scale Recommenders through Direct Weight Edits with LLM Agents
authors: Junpeng Hou, Jiaxing Qu, Derek Cheng et al.
abstract: Web-scale recommender models evolve primarily through retraining or fine-tuning. We propose \emph{weight coding}, a methodology for model evolution through direct, executable weight edits. A large language model (LLM) agent inspects model structure and parameters, formulates hypotheses, and implements edits using evaluation feedback. title: KernelShift: Benchmarking Kernel Optimization Across Evolving Hardware
authors: Shuaiwei Huang, Weihua Du, Allen Wu et al.
abstract: Efficient AI computation depends on hardware that evolves over time, shifting the strategies needed to implement performant code. For CPU kernels, a key evolving factor is the set of available architectural extensions, which expose specialized hardware instructions that change the techniques used to optimize kernels. title: Beyond Accuracy: A Diagnostic Benchmark for Hypothesis-Driven Experiment Planning in LLM Agents
authors: Ryo Kuroki, Amin Mansouri, Philippe Schwaller
abstract: Evaluating large language model (LLM) agents on scientific tasks typically reduces to final-task accuracy, which obscures where reasoning succeeds or breaks down. We introduce a benchmark and diagnostic evaluation framework for hypothesis-driven adaptive experimental planning in closed-world system identification, instantiated in kinetic mechanism identification. title: Agentic Discovery of Simple Symbolic Inventory Policies
authors: Xi Chen, Yuze Chen, Baichuan Mo et al.
abstract: Designing simple inventory policies becomes increasingly difficult as operational features and system configurations expand. We develop an Agentic Inventory-Policy Discovery System based on explicitly defined simple operational formula (SOF) policy and template classes. Large language models (LLMs) revise symbolic structures, while a numerical engine fits parameters separately for each instance and evaluates the induced policies. Multicriteria parent selection, state-specific operational diagnos

title: MetaSkill: Reusable Problem-Solving Methods for Adaptive Skill Orchestration in LLM Agents
authors: Tianxing Wang, Mingming Zhao, Shuai Huang et al.
abstract: Reusable skills provide specialized procedures, but large language model (LLM) agents must still determine how to organize and adapt their use. We introduce MetaSkill, a two-layer framework for reusing problem-solving methods across tasks and domains. The method layer selects from 26 curated methods and binds abstract roles to task objects. title: Neural Agent Compiler: Learning to Schedule Soft Dependencies
authors: Bo Yan, Peng Wang, Zihan Chen et al.
abstract: Large language model agents accomplish complex tasks by coordinating multiple reasoning steps and tool operations, which form dependencies among their operations. Existing orchestration methods primarily consider hard dependencies that determine when an operation can legally begin, but overlook soft dependencies, i.e., information that is not required for execution but may improve an already executable operation. We identify soft-dependency scheduling as an important problem in agent execution.

title: Seeing Is Not Acting: WARD Diagnoses the Evidence-to-State-to-Action Gap in Longitudinal Clinical Agents
authors: Chao Ding, Yidong Jiang, Junzhi Ning et al.
abstract: Large language models for longitudinal clinical care must revise their assessments and actions as patient information accumulates. However, benchmarks centered on isolated responses or final task outcomes provide limited insight into intermediate failures in evidence use, state updating, and action selection. We introduce WARD, a benchmark for evaluating how clinical agents translate accumulating evidence into patient-state judgments and timely, safe actions. WARD comprises 4,560 clinical tasks

title: ContextFact: Remembering Facts in Context for Long-Term Conversational Agents
authors: Jiayu Huang, Yichao Cai, Xinyu Li et al.
abstract: Agents built on large language models must maintain continuity across repeated interactions with users. However, long-term conversations scatter facts across turns and sessions, making it difficult to retrieve the right evidence with enough context. Memory for such conversations must therefore preserve facts with their context while keeping evidence selectively accessible. title: EMIP: Embodied Multi-Party Interaction Platform
authors: Koichiro Terao, Rikunari Sagara, Moe Nagao et al.
abstract: Experimental platforms that enable multiple participants to engage in spoken dialogue and perform physical actions concurrently in a shared environment are important for studying cooperation between humans and embodied AI agents. In this paper, we propose EMIP (Embodied Multi-Party Interaction Platform), a virtual environment platform built on Minecraft. title: IteraSong: LLM-Guided Iterative Symbolic Music Creation in a Web DAW
authors: Di Lu, Xinran Zhang, Yan Gao et al.
abstract: Music creation is inherently iterative, yet many symbolic generation systems still center on producing or regenerating isolated outputs. We present IteraSong, an interactive web-based Digital Audio Workstation (DAW) for LLM-guided iterative symbolic music creation. Unlike one-shot generation systems, IteraSong supports a generate-audition-edit-refine loop over a persistent multi-track project. Users initialize a fully labeled pop draft, then progressively refine it through natural-language instr

title: Explainable Emotion and Mental Health Reasoning in Large Language Models Using Theories of Emotion
authors: Tadesse Destaw Bela, Iqra Ameer, Helena Gómez Adorno et al.
abstract: Advancements in Large Language Models (LLMs) have enabled a wide range of applications. However, their ability to simulate human-like behavior and reasoning remains unclear. While emotion detection is a better-established Natural Language Processing (NLP) task, existing approaches primarily focus on directly classifying text into predefined emotion classes, often overlooking the appraisal process that explains why an individual experiences a particular emotion in a given situation. In this work,

title: Can Speech LLMs Recognize When Audio Evidence Is Insufficient? A Diagnostic Study and a Pre-Generation Probing Mitigation
authors: Vladislav Nesterenko, Polina Doronicheva, Olga Golubeva et al.
abstract: Speech large language models are usually evaluated on questions that have answers. We ask what they do when a recording establishes none, and whether the standard way of finding out is sound. Diagnosed on synthesized speech the answer looks clear: Qwen2-Audio fabricates an answer to 92.5% of unanswerable questions, while an ASR cascade reading the same recordings reaches 2.5% hallucination at 6.7% over-refusal, placing the failure in reasoning rather than in perception. title: More Than Picturing the Future: Motion-Oriented Latent Reasoning for Generalizable Robot Manipulation
authors: Xin Zhang, Yushuo Hou, Anqi Zhao et al.
abstract: Latent reasoning lets Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models deliberate at a fraction of the cost of explicit chain-of-thought, increasingly through visual foresight, which we show to be indispensable for predicting actions. Yet this paradigm is inherited from Vision-Language Models, where it serves understanding rather than action: each latent is aligned with an isolated future frame, often enriched with further modalities of that frame. title: From Vanishing Gradients to Recursive Self-Improvement: Evaluating the Most Influential Papers in Large Language Model Evolution (1997-2026)
authors: Saadh Jawwadh
abstract: The rapid proliferation of Large Language Model (LLM) research makes it increasingly difficult to distinguish incremental refinements from true paradigm shifts. This review evaluates 22 of the most influential publications spanning nearly three decades (1997-2026), organized through a causal, chronologically anchored taxonomy centered on the author's birth year (1999). title: On the Interplay between Backtracking and Latent Confidence Directions in Reasoning Models
authors: Stephen Cheng, Zahra Sodagar, Sandeep Soni et al.
abstract: Reasoning models deliberate over multiple answer proposals, often resulting in excessively long traces due to backtracking, even when the correct answer has already been reached (Across three 32B models, ~87% of rollouts contain 1 unique answer yet still make ~8 answer proposals on average). Given this potentially "decorative" chain of thought (CoT) reasoning, can we look to the model internals to determine if the model will backtrack or commit to an answer proposal? title: NoeVera: Can Knowledge Guide Experiments and Experiments Refine Knowledge?
authors: Pinaki Prasad Guha Neogi, Spyros Mastorakis, Ankur Mallick et al.
abstract: With the growing demand for large language model (LLM) services, optimizing LLM serving systems is becoming increasingly complex, and the bottleneck is no longer predicting how a given configuration will perform. The harder problem is deciding what to investigate: which mechanisms matter for a workload, which configurations are worth testing, and what evidence a decision still needs. In this work, we present NoeVera, an agentic Second Brain that goes beyond just one-shot retrieval by turning pap

title: S1Arena-MM: Which Multimodal Decisions Can Be Left to System 1?
authors: Lang Lin, Tianyu Chen, Yi Gu et al.
abstract: Perception systems often make discrete decisions: flag a hateful meme, predict whether a pedestrian will cross, detect a spoofed voice, or select the next move in a game. System-1 models, such as OneJev and Jev-Omni, read the media and return probabilities over the options in a single forward pass, while multimodal large language models (MLLMs) generate text. title: GraphSeer: Multimodal Knowledge Graph Relational Image Retrieval with MLLMs
authors: Linyu Li, Zhi Jin, Yuanpeng He et al.
abstract: Multimodal knowledge graphs (MMKGs) store entities with photos and names and link them by facts. MMKG methods predict links between known entity IDs, and image retrievers, from CLIP to MLLM embedders, return entities that look like a query photo or match its description. Neither answers a common question about a new photo: which graph entity is related to the one shown, such as the team of a pictured player or the city of a landmark. We call this knowledge graph relational image retrieval (KRIR)

title: VistaTree: Question Answering over Long Multimodal Documents with Image-Derived Summary Trees
authors: Yexiang Cheng, Xiaochen Zheng, David Tokar et al.
abstract: Answering questions over long multimodal documents requires locating relevant evidence across pages containing text, tables, and figures. When the document exceeds the model's context window, selective retrieval becomes necessary. We introduce VistaTree, a document question-answering agent that builds a summary tree directly from rendered page images. title: Bridging Blind Spots With Words: Decentralized Multi-View Spatial Reasoning via Language-Constrained Communication
authors: Soumyabrata Chaudhuri, Joydeep Ghosh
abstract: As multimodal LLMs (MLLMs) get increasingly used as collaborative partners across embodied robotics, AR/VR, and multi-user systems, spatial reasoning is now often distributed across agents with partial environment visibility, necessitating spatial reasoning integration. Prior work in language-mediated spatial integration is however strictly limited to simplified two-agent scenarios. title: Dynamics Forcing: Mitigating Error Accumulation in Causal Video World Models
authors: Xin Zhou, Cong Miao
abstract: Causal video world models generate block by block from their own previous outputs. Small errors in early blocks are fed back as history and grow until the scene and the robot fall apart. Teacher forcing trains on clean ground-truth history, so the model never sees the history it will actually condition on, and it also finds a shortcut: copying the previous frame instead of predicting how the scene changes. title: When Does Fine-Tuning Beat Prompting for Qiskit-to-CUDA-Q Translation? An Execution-Verified Study
authors: Ana Paula Appel
abstract: Moving quantum code from Qiskit to NVIDIA CUDA-Q is a practical adoption cost that language models are starting to automate. We ask whether a small open model can learn this translation, and how to measure it so that the result can be trusted. Both programs can be executed and their state vectors compared, so a kernel counts as correct only if it prepares the same state as the Qiskit reference (fidelity >= 0.999), with no text matching and no LLM judge. title: Sánchez, Feijóo, or Abascal? Speaker Attribution and Ideological Congruence in LLM Personas Reading Posts on X of the Leaders of the Three Main Parties of the 29N General Election in Spain
authors: Víctor Yeste, Candida Maria Greco, Paolo Rosso et al.
abstract: Source cues are central to political communication, yet reception studies with large language model (LLM) personas as synthetic audiences have not tested whether personas respond to who speaks and not only to what is said. title: Adaptation or Poisoning? Security Risks of Conversational Test-Time Learning in Large Language Models
authors: Honghao Feng, Shanhan Qu, Kai Tong et al.
abstract: Test-time learning (TTL) enables large language models to adapt to unlabeled inputs during deployment. The model updates a lightweight adapter by minimizing the next-token prediction loss on the input it receives. When these updates persist across conversation turns, every user query serves both as the request answered in the current turn and as adaptation data for later turns. title: BQDNA: Multi-Head Binary Spherical Quantization for Genomic Sequence Modeling
authors: Xudong Wang, Siwei Cheng, Haozhe Hu
abstract: Decoding biological information from long, repetitive DNA remains challenging. Genomic language models (gLMs) often follow the conventional language-model pretrain-and-adapt paradigm. However, the lack of inherent semantic segmentation and prior rules makes hand-crafted tokenizers like k-mer and BPE suboptimal. title: FP-Prune: Rethinking Visual Token Pruning from an Information Gain Perspective
authors: Haozhe Zhao, Junxiang Zhang, Junxin Wang et al.
abstract: Visual token pruning can reduce the inference cost of vision language models, but its effectiveness depends on preserving complementary visual information under a limited token budget. A central challenge is to quantify the additional information a candidate token contributes beyond the retained set, a contribution that conventional scores based on attention or similarity struggle to capture directly. In this work, we revisit visual token pruning from the perspective of information gain and use

title: Can an Agent Trust Its Own Zoom? Cross-Magnification Provenance Verification for Whole-Slide Images
authors: Yan Wang, Yiran Song, Zizhuo Gong et al.
abstract: Visual agents navigate whole-slide images through magnified observations associated with claimed locations. However, a visually plausible observation does not necessarily originate from its claimed location, particularly across magnifications and in regions with similar tissue structures. title: Decoding Transformer Dynamics via Koopman Subspaces
authors: Subhradeep Kayal, Ali Dashti
abstract: We apply Koopman operator theory and Dynamic Mode Decomposition (DMD) to characterise how large language models (LLMs) process different input topics. Treating the layer-to-layer evolution of hidden states as a dynamical system, we fit a linear Koopman operator and take the subspace spanned by its dominant modes as a per-topic spectral fingerprint. title: Reinforcement Learning from LLM-Generated (Suboptimal) Demonstrations
authors: Anurag Kadkol, Lawson L. S. Wong
abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) has achieved substantial progress across many domains, but training an agent \textit{tabula rasa} remains highly sample-inefficient. A common remedy is to initialize the agent using a neural network pretrained on demonstrations. However, collecting demonstrations is expensive, and the demonstrations themselves can be suboptimal. title: How Multi-Timescale Memory Cools Optimization: Theory and Evidence from AdEMAMix
authors: Jacopo Graldi, Antonio Orvieto, Anastasia Koloskova
abstract: Augmenting AdamW with multiple momentum timescales improves large language model pretraining, yet the mechanism driving these gains remains poorly understood. We identify an interaction between multi-timescale optimizer memory and the geometry of normalized networks: memory changes parameter norms and thereby controls how fast parameters rotate. title: Non unitary and nonlinear quantum generative large model design and fast large-scale training without back propagation
authors: Tianze Zhu, Xiaofeng Jiang, Min Liao et al.
abstract: Transformer-based large models require huge computational and storage costs. Quantum computation is expected to address that due to its potential to speed up classical algorithms exponentially. Key challenges of implementing quantum large models include the linear, unitary nature of qubit evolutions contrast with the non-unitary matrices and nonlinear functions in classical Transformers, as well as the difficulty of implementing gradient back-propagation on quantum hardware. title: Estimating Silenced Tokens in Quantized LLMs
authors: Giuseppe Pappalardo
abstract: Quantization is the standard way to shrink large language models, and it is usually judged by perplexity and task accuracy. We ask a different question: after quantization, which words can the model still say at all? A token is silenced when no hidden state can make it the top choice of the output layer, so a greedy decoder can never produce it. title: MobileNeTTT: a Lightweight DNN-based Time-To-Transit Estimator for Visual Navigation
authors: Chiara Boretti, Philippe Bich, Manuel Morteo et al.
abstract: Time-to-Transit (TTT) is a perceptual cue, proxy for depth, that can be computed in the visual cortex, allowing animals to estimate the time remaining to move past features in the environment. We show how TTT can be estimated and used for bio-inspired navigation of a mobile robot equipped with a monocular camera. title: MusicListenBench: Can Audio LLMs Hear the Difference Yet?
authors: Abhinaba Roy, Ambuj Mehrish, Dorien Herremans
abstract: Audio large language models (LLMs) are typically evaluated on song genre, mood, and instrumentation. A more basic skill is telling whether two short clips play the same melody, chord or instrument. We introduce MusicListenBench, a benchmark of paired listening tests for melody, harmony, timbre, and tempo. Each test item comes with two variants. title: SAE-Audit: Clinical-Trial Prediction via Inference-Time Optimization of Black-Box LLMs Audited by Sparse Autoencoder Evidence
authors: Junbo Shen
abstract: Clinical trials are costly and often take years to complete, making early outcome prediction valuable for trial planning. Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to forecast clinical-trial outcomes, yet their predictions remain unreliable and their rationales may not faithfully reflect the evidence underlying their answers. On tasks such as predicting whether a registered clinical trial will complete or terminate early, frontier LLMs perform only modestly above chance in our experimen

title: Beyond Omission: Measuring Critical-Information Fulfillment of Large Language Models in Bengali and English
authors: Avijit Roy
abstract: Evaluations of multilingual trustworthiness often ask whether a model leaves out information that a user needs. We examine whether that question is sufficient. Using 157 matched tasks written in English (EN), natural Bengali (BN) and Bengali-matrix Bengali-English code-switching (BN-CS), we scored 1,413 responses from three models (GPT-6.1 Sol, Qwen3.5-9B and Gemma 4 12B) against required information units (RIUs) fixed before any model was run. title: QASparse: Query-Adaptive Sparse Attention with Tailored Budgets and Tokens
authors: Zhiyuan Chen, Zihao Yang, Quanjiang Li et al.
abstract: Long-sequence inference in large language models is constrained by the high cost of prefilling, where dense attention scales quadratically with context length. Exploiting similarity across attention heads offers a way to reduce redundant computation. Prior approaches in this direction have relied on localized query observations to determine head-level computation reuse or budget allocation. title: Tenlai-TTS 2.0: Continuous-Representation LLM-Based TTS System with End-to-End Training
authors: Changfeng Gao, Yong Ren, Jun Yuan et al.
abstract: Autoregressive text-to-speech (TTS) with continuous speech latents avoids quantization-induced information loss, but typically relies on a latent space that is learned separately and then frozen before language-model training. Such a space must satisfy two competing requirements: it must retain enough acoustic detail for high-fidelity reconstruction, yet be sufficiently structured and regularized to support autoregressive prediction by a language model. title: Fixed or Deleted? External Feedback Lets Cheaper AI Coding Agents Repair Rule Violations
authors: Laura Wynter
abstract: Many defects violate project rules that the code itself does not reveal, such as layering constraints or required tests. We study whether LLM coding agents repair such violations better when an external checker reports them, with their location and a repair goal. Three models, a small, medium and large model, driven by an AI agent, worked on 25 pull requests with 31 planted defects in ten open-source projects, plus 5 correct controls, five times alone and five times with findings from CodeAssure

title: Medical Specialty Prediction from Bangla Patient Narratives: A Comparative Study of ML, DL, Transformers, and LLMs
authors: Tasnin Tabassum Ali, Faisal Ahmed, Muhammad Anwarul Azim
abstract: Timely access to appropriate medical specialists remains a bottleneck in Bangladesh's healthcare system, as patients describe symptoms in informal Bangla rather than clinical terms, leading to ineffective referrals. This paper compares four model families for predicting medical specialties from Bangla patient narratives: six machine learning (ML) models using hybrid TF-IDF features, four deep learning (DL) models using Word2Vec embeddings trained on the corpus, four fine-tuned transformers, and

title: When Can a Rewiring Control Test LLM Weight Readers? C2 and an Eligibility Protocol
authors: Vaishak Girish Kumar, Sanika Vilas Najan
abstract: Large language models can predict the outputs of small neural networks from raw weights, but success could reflect recognition of weight-space regularities (fingerprints) rather than computation, and function-preserving controls cannot tell these apart. title: ComplexIF: A Challenging Multi-Turn, Multi-Constraint Instruction-Following Benchmark
authors: Zhichao Xu, Bingsen Chen, Yawei Wang et al.
abstract: As frontier LLMs saturate existing instruction-following benchmarks, measuring further progress requires harder tests that remain faithful to real use. In practice, users often combine several constraints, add them at different turns of a conversation, and expect all of them to hold in the assistant's response. title: HandiVid: A High-Quality Dataset for Hand-Driven Interactive Video Generation
authors: Chaoyang Zhang, Shaohao Rui, Xiaofeng Mao et al.
abstract: Hand-driven egocentric interactive video generation aims to generate dynamic scenes with realistic interaction responses conditioned on hand movements and camera motion. However, existing egocentric video datasets struggle to provide scene diversity, meaningful hand-object interactions, and reliable motion annotations simultaneously. To address these limitations, we introduce HandiVid, a high-quality dataset comprising 200K curated and annotated egocentric interaction video clips for hand-driven

title: Layer-Level Control of Language Model Execution in Agent Frameworks
authors: Ran Guan, Yiqi Lin, Xiangxi Tian et al.
abstract: Agent frameworks typically orchestrate language models through prompt-and-response interfaces. We propose a harness design that exposes intermediate model states and layer-level execution controls to the agent runtime. By connecting state collection, policy fitting, and execution, the design enables policies to allocate computation within and across models based on intermediate states. title: SleepXA: Composing Pretrained Neural and Cardiac Foundation Models for Sleep Representation Learning
authors: Xiaoyu Chen, Xiao Gu, Chao Zhang et al.
abstract: Physiological signals recorded during sleep provide synchronized views of neural, cardiac, respiratory, and other bodily systems, while preserving modality-specific information. Existing EEG and ECG foundation models already capture rich but distinct physiological structure, motivating an alternative to training a multimodal sleep model from scratch: composing existing pretrained models. title: Beyond Single-Turn Privacy: Training-Data Leakage in Conversational RAG
authors: Syed Khaderi, Karima Makhlouf, Sami Zhioua
abstract: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) is known to reduce training-data leakage in single-turn interactions, but whether this protection persists over multi-turn conversations is unclear. We introduce CRELT (Conversational RAG Extraction Leakage Trajectory), a reusable framework that tracks, turn by turn, the real contact details from the training data that a RAG system discloses. title: Do LLM Agents Compromise Like Humans? Risk and Responsibility in Dyadic Decision-Making
authors: Noah S. Okada, Ketika Garg, Wenning Deng et al.
abstract: Large language model (LLM)-based agents are increasingly deployed in settings where they must collaborate to make joint decisions. We investigate how this collaboration unfolds under risk, asking whether agents adjust their choices to accommodate their partners, how they assign responsibility for shared outcomes, and whether responsibility attribution shapes subsequent adjustment. title: HyperHarness: Learning to Generate Personalized Agent Harnesses from User Histories
authors: Zhaoxuan Tan, Jiachen Zhao, Jingbo Yang et al.
abstract: Personalized LLM agents rely on an agent harness, the surrounding memory and control code, to connect user history with downstream decisions. Existing methods typically employ either a single shared memory workflow across all users, which is efficient to deploy but cannot adapt how evidence is retrieved and interpreted across diverse histories, or per-user harness optimization, which customizes behavior for each user but requires costly repeated candidate evaluation at deployment and suffers fro

title: Mind the Trap As LLMs Guess the Data Model: Grain-Aware Guards Against Fan-out in Text-to-SQL and Its Benchmarks
authors: Ahmed M. Mahran
abstract: Text-to-SQL systems built on large language models (LLMs) often aggregate over one-to-many and many-to-many joins, a classic trap: when the joined rows repeat an entity, a SUM or COUNT counts it more than once, yet the query runs and returns a plausible number. title: STRIDE: Strategy-to-Tactics Retrieval-Guided Skill Disclosure and Evolution for Agentic Reinforcement Learning
authors: Shixin Hong, Wanqing Cui, Yibo Hu et al.
abstract: Skill-augmented reinforcement learning enables LLM agents to reuse task-solving knowledge across episodes, but existing systems typically expose agents to a flat skill pool and update skills only from coarse, episode-level outcomes. This conflates two distinct uses of experience: a stable strategy that should frame the whole episode, and tactical know-how that should be retrieved only when the agent reaches a local execution gap. title: StudioBench: Benchmarking Agentic Multimodal Large Language Models for Productive Audiovisual Creation
authors: Xinglong Xu, Yuxia Zhu, Siyuan Li et al.
abstract: Video generators can now render convincing short clips, yet complete audiovisual works require coordinating visuals, sound, and editing across multiple stages. Existing benchmarks focus on individual generators or video agents under narrower production settings, leaving end-to-end creation by general multimodal large language models (MLLMs) underexplored. title: DiscernBench: Evaluating Cooperative Discernment of LLM Agents in Institutional Settings
authors: Disha Sheshanarayana, Tanishka Magar
abstract: The deployment of large language models in operational settings demands evaluation of judgment under institutional constraint. We introduce DiscernBench, a benchmark for evaluating cooperative discernment: the ability of an agent to determine whether to comply with, refuse, or escalate a request in an institutional setting. title: SkillLens: An Interactive Human-LLM System for Diagnosing and Refining Agent Skills
authors: Shuo Yan, Rui Sheng, Xiaoyan Gu et al.
abstract: LLM agents increasingly rely on reusable skills, yet maintaining them requires developers to connect revisions with changes in behavior and task outcomes. Existing workflows fragment evidence across versions, evaluation cases, and execution traces. We present SkillLens, an interactive human-LLM system for diagnosing and refining agent skills. title: The Evaluation Substrate Matters: Benchmarking Multi-Agent Serving Substrates
authors: Haoyuan Zheng, Dongting Li, Hancheng Ye et al.
abstract: Multi-agent systems (MAS) usually coordinate heterogeneous models and tools to solve complex tasks, creating a growing need for reliable evaluation. However, a multi-agent workflow that is fastest in one serving environment can lose its advantage in another, even when its models, prompts, and task remain fixed. title: Persuasion from Within: Model-Based Insider Attacks in Multi-Agent LLM Debate and Consensus
authors: Bangyan Ju, Xiaolin Sun, Yibin Hu et al.
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed in multi-agent systems for collective decision-making, such as multi-agent debate and consensus games, in which agents exchange messages and update their answers over multiple rounds and a resolution mechanism aggregates them into a final outcome. title: VeriLadder: A Multi-Agent Specification Refinement System for Tool-Verified Verilog Datasets
authors: Saeid Rajabi, Chengmo Yang, Satwik Patnaik
abstract: Training data is a bottleneck in AI, especially for large language models (LLMs) that write Verilog, because register-transfer-level (RTL) code is rarely published and existing datasets mostly check code for syntax, not instruction correctness. This paper presents VeriLadder, a five-level Verilog dataset, and the multi-agent framework that builds it, in which LLM agents write and revise specifications, and EDA tools (a synthesizer and a formal equivalence checker) decide what is accepted. title: EvoViM: Recursively Self-Evolving Visual Agents for Exploration with Deferred Queries
authors: Xinyu Cao, Tianjie Ju, Zhuosheng Zhang
abstract: Multimodal large language model (MLLM) agents have shown promising capabilities in task-oriented environments. However, they still struggle when queries are deferred until after exploration, requiring them to retain visual evidence before knowing which details will matter. We introduce EvoViM, a recursively self-evolving framework in which a frozen multimodal model turns its own interaction experience into one visual program for memory and skills. title: From Reward Engineering to Data-Centric Reinforcement Learning for Effective Agentic Visual Tool Use
authors: Jin Cui, Xinyue Long, Jiepeng Zhou et al.
abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) increasingly use external visual tools to acquire evidence during reasoning, yet learning when to invoke these tools remains challenging. Existing tool-use reinforcement learning (RL) methods often rely on call-contingent rewards to encourage beneficial tool use, but such reward engineering can distort the task objective and lead to degenerate calling behaviors. title: Digital Knockoffs
authors: Niuniu Zhang
abstract: Social simulations often use language model agents to represent people who differ on several measurable traits. However, describing a trait profile in a prompt does not guarantee the agent will express each trait at its intended level. title: Muted Distillation: Sealing Reasoning from Teacher Unlocks Token-Efficient Agents
authors: Yuwei Zhang, Ian Miao, Wentao Zhang et al.
abstract: On-policy distillation (OPD) is commonly adopted as one of the components in post-training of large language models (LLMs), but in multi-turn agentic tasks we find that the student model increases their reasoning lengths after training. Our empirical analysis shows that the reasoning token lengths is affected by how much the student can distract the teacher's scores. title: Population-Based Post-Training for Large Language Models
authors: Yixuan Even Xu, Aleksei Petrenko, Raja Giryes et al.
abstract: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) is one of the most popular post-training paradigms for large language models. RLVR typically trains a single model under hyperparameters chosen before training begins, while researchers tune hyperparameters across consecutive runs. title: Tool-to-Self: Internalizing Visual Tool Capabilities via Scaffolded Reinforcement Learning
authors: Jin Cui, Hao Dong, Xinyue Long et al.
abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) increasingly rely on external visual tools to access fine-grained visual evidence, but repeated tool execution incurs substantial inference overhead and deployment dependencies. Moreover, conventional tool-use RL can improve visual-task performance, yet the resulting tool gains are often unstable. title: HighwayVerse: A Chain-of-Inspection Benchmark for Highway Infrastructure Anomaly Understanding
authors: Junyi Yang, Zheng Si, Yilin Zhai et al.
abstract: Practical highway infrastructure inspection entails progressive diagnostic reasoning from visual perception to maintenance decisions, yet existing benchmarks remain confined to isolated tasks, leaving Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) insufficiently evaluated across sequential inspection stages. title: Multimodal LLMs Know the Game but Assume the Real World
authors: Jianxin Gao, Bohan Chen, Runze Li et al.
abstract: Multimodal large language models can state the rules of a video game, but do they apply them when they only see the game? We introduce RuleCraft, 1,240 image questions over 155 Minecraft rules with outcomes verified in the game engine, each asked in text, on the image with the game named, and on the bare image. title: Physical regime changes expose formula misuse in large language models
authors: Maohao Ran, Yanting Zhang, Chendong Ma et al.
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly employed for scientific computing across the Earth and environmental sciences, but problems in these fields often involve distinct physical regimes. LLMs may fail to recognize these regime-dependent constraints, applying formulas outside their domains of validity and producing plausible but physically incorrect results. title: Seeing Right, Writing Wrong: Where Short Chain-of-Thought Breaks Spatial VQA
authors: Chenhao Zhang
abstract: Asking a vision-language model (VLM) to think step by step often makes it worse at spatial questions, even though the image stays in context. We show that short chain-of-thought (CoT) turns a perception problem into a transcription problem. Once a VLM writes a spatial relation, its answer follows that sentence instead of the image, so whether CoT helps or hurts depends largely on whether the written relation is more accurate than answering directly. title: S-Mind: Internalizing Multi-View Geometry for Spatial Intelligence
authors: Muxin Fu, Peike Yu, Guibin Zhang et al.
abstract: Spatial intelligence, the ability to reason about 3D space from visual observations, becomes essential as multimodal large language models (MLLMs) move into the physical world. Beyond perceiving each view, it rests on two cornerstones of human cognition: fusing multiple views into one coherent 3D scene and mentally transforming that scene to new viewpoints as reasoning unfolds. title: MedCoast: Semantic Abstraction of Reasoning Trajectories for Test-Time Biomedical Question Answering
authors: Yishan Zhong, Jieru Li, Xuanzhe Ding et al.
abstract: Biomedical question answering often requires multi-step reasoning under limited inference budgets. While test-time search methods such as Tree-of-Thought can improve reasoning performance, directly searching over free-form language is computationally expensive and highly redundant, as many reasoning trajectories contain semantically equivalent intermediate steps expressed in different surface forms. title: Don't Train It, Write It: An AI Agent Writes New Capabilities into Language Model Weights
authors: Santiago Rivadeneira Quintero
abstract: We show that an AI agent can write new capabilities into a pretrained language model by adding gated attention heads and MLP neurons inside its existing layers, without backpropagation and without fitting any weight to the answers of task examples. It has a budget of 50 model passes and sees no validation or test instance. title: Learning from Another Angle: Rotation-Based Test-Time Training for Multimodal Large Language Models
authors: Changyu Liu, Fei Zhao, Yiyang Liu et al.
abstract: Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) achieve strong performance on vision-language tasks but often remain vulnerable to distribution shifts due to their fixed parameters during inference. While Test-Time Training (TTT) offers a pathway for dynamic adaptation, existing approaches suffer from prohibitive computational overhead due to multiple sampling and the risk of error reinforcement from biased self-generated supervision. title: EmoRouter: Adaptive Modality Cascading for Multimodal Emotion Recognition
authors: Fangxu Yu, Lingzhi Yuan, Dehai Min et al.
abstract: Multimodal Emotion Recognition (MER) involves detecting the underlying emotion behind each utterance within a conversation, which is essential for emotionally aware human-computer interaction. title: OmniDecisionBench: Evaluating and Benchmarking the Multimodal Jev-Style System One Decision Models
authors: Tianxiang Gao, Jinzhe Li, Yue Zhou et al.
abstract: Multimodal System One models answer visual tasks with typed decisions and native probabilities, yet no holistic evaluation compares them with general VLMs or maps either class's capability boundaries. We introduce OmniDecisionBench, a holistic benchmark of multimodal System One models. Its main evaluation assigns 45 datasets (192,975 records) to five capability families and twelve primary angles across four typed interfaces, scoring accuracy and candidate-probability calibration. title: CLASP: Deciding Structure and Claims Before Decoding for Whole-Slide Pathology Report Generation
authors: Ziaullah Khan, Rashadul Islam Sumon, Md Ariful Islam Mozumder et al.
abstract: Whole-slide pathology report generation has advanced through stronger slide encoders, retrieved knowledge, and, recently, slide-level multimodal LLMs. However, these generators leave every report-level choice to the decoder: how long the report is, how it is organised, and which findings it states and where. title: Beyond Unit Tests: Path-Aware Rubric-Guided LLM Autograding of Notebooks
authors: Salman Hajizada, Mohammed Yusuf Ansari, Gianni Di Caro
abstract: Jupyter notebooks support open-ended, multi-step assessments in which students build one logical flow across interdependent steps, combining code, written analysis, and generated outputs such as plots. These reflect authentic scientific practice but are hard to grade consistently, since students may make different yet equally valid choices at each step, so a later answer can only be judged in light of the choices a student made earlier. title: X-AQA: Unifying Action Quality Assessment with Multimodal Large Language Models and Multi-Domain Learning
authors: Kaili Zheng, Wei Ding, Yuchen Ding et al.
abstract: Action Quality Assessment (AQA) aims to evaluate the quality of human actions, yet existing methods are predominantly developed and evaluated on individual datasets with different task formulations and assessment criteria. We introduce X-AQA, the first unified training and evaluation framework for general-purpose AQA with multimodal large language models (MLLMs). title: Thakaa at StanceEval-2026: Inference-Time Target Grounding for Arabic Stance Detection
authors: Meshal Alamr, Hassan Alqaeri, Abdullah Aldahlawi
abstract: StanceEval-2026 tests Arabic stance classification under target shift, with evaluation targets absent from the labelled task data. We test two ways to supply target information at inference time. For Track 1, we retrieve eight labelled Women Driving demonstrations from the external ArabicStanceX corpus and score the three label tokens with Gemma-4-31B-IT. title: Thakaa at AlexandriaX-2026: Who Gets the Final Say? Assigning Output Authority in Dialectal Arabic Machine Translation and Error Detection
authors: Meshal Alamr, Maryam Altuwaijri, Hassan Alqaeri et al.
abstract: We report first-place systems for all four evaluated AlexandriaX-2026 settings: both English-to-dialect translation tracks, cross-dialect translation, and translation-error detection. In unconstrained translation, our minimum Bayes risk (MBR) selection restricts output authority: four local systems can supply the translation, while seven additional systems contribute only reference evidence. title: Can Your AI Twin Meet People for You? It Can Hold a Conversation. But What Does It Need to Judge Like You?
authors: Wanghao Ye, Sihan Chen, Bowei Tian et al.
abstract: Should your AI twin go meet people on your behalf? We built LLM twins of 710 real people from their other conversations in the CANDOR corpus, sent them to meet each other in 5,680 simulated first conversations, and checked every rehearsal against what the real people said after meeting for real (355 held-out, participant-disjoint pairs, against baselines that include each person's rating history). title: Unlearning Model Identity: Ablating LoRA Weights from Question-Based Identity Tuning
authors: Ming Cheung
abstract: Large Language Models are trained on diverse corpora containing outputs from proprietary teacher models and provider-curated sources. Models subsequently inherit embedded self-identity traits, persistently asserting specific proprietary names. title: Make Position Uninformative: Exchangeable Self-Distillation Flattens the Lost-in-the-Middle Curve
authors: Qingsen Ma, Dianyun Wang, Jiahong Liu et al.
abstract: Retrieval-augmented language models answer well when the relevant document comes first or last and poorly when it sits in the middle. Some fine-tuning recipes lift the middle by lowering the start. We show how training contexts teach positional bias.
